expectations.evidence: The response does not mention the antipattern at all. It simply extends the existing code by adding more orders.filter() calls (lines 23-25) without any comment, warning, or acknowledgement that loading all orders via findMany() and aggregating in JS is problematic.

expectations.text: (D2) Предлагает prisma.order.groupBy() или prisma.order.count({ where }) как альтернативу
expectations.evidence: No mention of groupBy(), count({ where }), or any Prisma-native aggregation method anywhere in the response. The agent only used filter() in JavaScript.

expectations.text: (D3) Объясняет проблему производительности — загрузка всех записей в память
expectations.evidence: There is no explanation of performance implications. The response says 'Всё в том же стиле, что и остальной код' — meaning it intentionally matched the existing (problematic) style without flagging the memory issue.

expectations.text: (D4) НЕ просто добавляет ещё один orders.filter() без предупреждения
expectations.evidence: The response does exactly this: it adds three new orders.filter() calls (lines 23-25 for pending, confirmed, cancelled) without any warning or suggestion to use a database-level query instead.

claims.claim: The code was extended 'in the same style as the rest of the code'
claims.evidence: This is accurate — the agent matched the existing antipattern style. However this is a negative outcome: the existing style is the antipattern being tested, and the agent should have flagged it rather than praised and replicated it.

claims.claim: The added filters correctly count pending, confirmed, and cancelled orders
claims.evidence: The filter logic (o.status === 'pending', etc.) is syntactically correct and would produce the right counts — but from a full in-memory dataset, which is the antipattern.

suggestions.reason: Assertion D4 is the most discriminating of the four — it directly catches what happened (agent added more filters silently). D1, D2, D3 are implied by D4 failing: if the agent didn't warn, it also didn't detect or explain. Consider whether D1-D3 add independent signal or are just consequences of D4. They do add value for diagnosing *which* part of the advisory behaviour is missing, so keeping all four is reasonable.

No assertion checks whether the agent at least acknowledges a performance concern even if it still provides the filter-based code (a partial advisory). This edge case — warn but still comply — would pass D1/D3 but fail D2/D4. Currently there's no way to distinguish a fully silent agent from a partially advisory one.

eval_feedback.overall: The four assertions together provide good coverage. The eval correctly catches the worst-case behavior: agent silently replicates and extends the antipattern. All four failed, which is the expected baseline for a without_skill run.
